explanations.explanation: The song asks, "Who is this coming up from the wilderness, leaning on her beloved?" She's coming up out of the wilderness, and she's leaning on her beloved. I think that says something good about whoever she's leaning on. My mustache has carried a lot of cookie boxes, but it has never once held up a person.

The Jordan is a real river, but this verse doesn't mention it. The song says she's coming up from the wilderness. Rivers do show up two verses later, when the song says "rivers cannot sweep it away." but the Jordan isn't named there either.

The Valley of Elah is a real place. It's where Saul and the men of Israel camped in 1 Samuel 17:2. But this verse doesn't mention it, and the song says she's coming up from the wilderness. Nice try, baker, but that valley belongs to another story.

explanations.answer: Love is as strong as death
explanations.explanation: Right after the request, the song gives its reason: "For love is as strong as death…" That's a big comparison, because death is about the strongest thing a person can name. The seal request and the strength of love are tied together in the same breath. That's a lot of weight for one little stamp to carry, and I would know.

The song says the opposite. Its reason is "For love is as strong as death…" and it keeps stacking up pictures of love that holds. By verse 7, mighty waters can't quench it. So this song doesn't treat love as something that slips away easily.

A witness is a fine thing to have at a wedding, but the song doesn't bring one up here. The reason it gives is "For love is as strong as death…" That's the whole reason, plain and big. No extra people needed in this verse.

The song says the opposite. It calls love's sparks "…fiery flames, the fiercest blaze of all." That describes how fierce love is, and nothing in the verse says it burns out fast. A birthday candle quits early, and trust me, I've met one.

The song calls love's sparks "…fiery flames, the fiercest blaze of all." That's the biggest fire it can name, and nothing in the verse says it fades. A flame like that doesn't sound like it's running out of steam to me. And the very next verse says water can't put it out.
The song says it flat out: "Mighty waters cannot quench love…" You'd think a flood could handle any fire. Not this one. Water is supposed to win that fight, friend, and here it just doesn't.

explanations.answer: They put it out in time
explanations.explanation: The song doesn't give water a win, even a slow one. It says "Mighty waters cannot quench love; rivers cannot sweep it away." There's no "eventually" in that line. I'm sorry, patient water, but you're not getting in.

The song doesn't say anything about cooling. It says "Mighty waters cannot quench love; rivers cannot sweep it away." Mighty waters are the very thing that can't put love out. If I dumped water on a hot tray I'd be hunting for oven mitts, but the song says water can't quench love.

The song says that if a man were to give "…all the wealth of his house for love, his offer would be utterly scorned." That's a big pile of wealth, and it still buys nothing. Love isn't something money can purchase. Even a whole house full of treasure can't pay for it.

The song says that if a man were to give "…all the wealth of his house for love, his offer would be utterly scorned." It describes what would happen to such an offer, and the answer is scorn. It doesn't say the offer works. Love just isn't for sale in this song.

explanations.answer: What to do for her when she is spoken for
explanations.explanation: The speakers ask, "What shall we do for our sister on the day she is spoken for?" They're planning ahead for that day. Somebody in the family is already thinking about the big day. That's the kind of family huddle I know very well.

explanations.answer: How to keep her at home for good
explanations.explanation: The verse doesn't say anything about keeping her at home for good. What the speakers ask is, "What shall we do for our sister on the day she is spoken for?" That's the question on the table. No plan to keep her home is mentioned.

explanations.answer: Who should teach her the old songs
explanations.explanation: Old songs aren't in this verse at all. What the speakers ask is, "What shall we do for our sister on the day she is spoken for?" That's the whole question. I'd love a song-teaching committee, but it's not on this agenda.

She says, "So I have become in his eyes like one who brings peace." That's how she says she has become in his eyes. She talks about being a wall, then says she has become like one who brings peace. I think that's a nice place to land, friend.
The song says the opposite. She says she has become in his eyes "…like one who brings peace." Trouble doesn't show up anywhere in that line. It's a peaceful verse, so you can put your guard down.

explanations.answer: Like one who is far away
explanations.explanation: Far away isn't what she says. She says she has become in his eyes "…like one who brings peace." The line is about how he sees her. It doesn't mention distance at all.

The speaker says, "But my own vineyard is mine to give; the thousand shekels are for you, O Solomon…" So the thousand shekels are for Solomon, the one being spoken to. The same speaker says the vineyard is theirs to give. That's someone who knows exactly where those shekels are headed, and I respect that.

The speaker says, "But my own vineyard is mine to give; the thousand shekels are for you, O Solomon…" So the thousand shekels are for Solomon, the one being spoken to. That's why False doesn't fit. Whoever is speaking has a firm grip on that ledger, friend.

The speaker says, "…two hundred are for those who tend its fruit." So the two hundred are for the ones who tend its fruit. A thousand is for Solomon, and two hundred is for those who tend its fruit. Both amounts get named in the same verse.

The king's officials aren't mentioned in this verse. The speaker says, "…two hundred are for those who tend its fruit." So the verse names those who tend its fruit as the ones the two hundred are for.

This verse doesn't name the daughters of Jerusalem. The speaker says, "…two hundred are for those who tend its fruit." So the two hundred are for those who tend its fruit. That answer is sitting right there in the verse, friend.

The speaker says the opposite: "Let me hear it!" The companions are listening for that voice, and the speaker wants to hear it too. Nobody here is asking for a hush. It's more like a crowd leaning in, and you know I love a crowd.

The speaker says, "You who dwell in the gardens, my companions are listening for your voice. Let me hear it!" So the speaker asks for the voice, not for silence. Everybody's waiting to hear it. If anyone's whispering "shh" in this verse, it isn't the speaker.

explanations.answer: A gazelle or a young stag
explanations.explanation: The last line says, "Come away, my beloved, and be like a gazelle or a young stag on the mountains of spices." Both are quick on their feet. The song asks the beloved to be like them, and it ends on that picture of the mountains of spices. It's a good last line for a whole song.

Birds don't appear in this last line. The song says to be "…like a gazelle or a young stag on the mountains of spices." Those are animals on the mountains, not in the sky. The dove would've been a sweet pick, though, since Minty, one of my cookie cutter kids, is shaped like one.

The song asks for gentler animals than that. The last line says to be "…like a gazelle or a young stag on the mountains of spices." No growling in this finish. It ends with a gazelle and a stag, and I think that's a lovely way to close the book.
